cultivar: Described for Wu Ye; the name may be used for other Dancong strains
processing: Winter leaf made as Dancong in general: withered, tossed for partial oxidation, fixed, rolled and dried. Winter leaf grows slowly and comes out stout.
harvest_season: Winter, the smallest picking of the year.
appearance_liquor: Typically orange-yellow, as with other Dancong.
appearance_wet: Typically thick leaves with reddened edges, as with other tossed Dancong.
taste_profile: Known above all for a strong aroma, the most intense of the year's pickings by Chinese accounts.

brewing.notes: General Dancong advice: plenty of leaf, hot water, quick pours.

vintage_note: Sold as the winter harvest of a stated year, in small lots. Ask which strain it is, since the name describes a picking rather than a tree.
description:
Xue Pian, snowflake, is less a strain than a season: the winter Dancong picking, described in Chinese accounts of the Wu Ye strain.

Cold weather slows the leaf, so it comes out stout, and yields are the lowest of any Dancong picking. Processing specific to winter leaf is not well documented here, so expect Dancong work in general.

The appeal is aroma, said to be the strongest of the year. Use plenty of leaf and quick pours.

Because Xue Pian describes a picking, the label should name the strain as well as the year. Small harvests invite stretching the name, so buy from someone who can say which trees it came from.
history: Little is documented about when the name came into use. Chinese descriptions of the Wu Ye strain explain it as the winter picking, named for its stout flake-like leaf and prized as the scarcest and most fragrant of the year.
